lessons.title: Measuring properly: tape measure, ruler, mm/cm/m, and reading between the marks
lessons.intro: Whether you're building a cubby, hanging a picture, or checking if the new bookshelf will actually fit, everything starts with a good measurement. Let's get the tape measure out.

sections.heading: Why measuring properly matters
sections.body:
Guessing a length might work sometimes, but it goes wrong just as often. A shelf cut too short leaves a gap. A curtain measured too long drags on the floor.

Measuring properly means using the right tool, lining it up correctly, and reading it carefully. It only takes a few extra seconds, and it saves you from redoing the job.

sections.heading: The units: millimetres, centimetres and metres
sections.body:
We measure length in **millimetres (mm)**, **centimetres (cm)** and **metres (m)**. They're all connected by tens.

- 10 mm = 1 cm
- 100 cm = 1 m
- 1000 mm = 1 m

Small, fiddly things like a screw or a gap in a hinge are usually measured in millimetres. A book or a picture frame is usually measured in centimetres. A hallway or a piece of decking is usually measured in metres.

example.prompt: A plank is 2.4 m long. How many centimetres is that?

sections.heading: Reading between the marks
sections.body:
Look closely at a ruler or tape measure and you'll see big numbers for whole centimetres, and lots of small tick marks in between. Each of those small ticks is 1 millimetre.

When something doesn't line up exactly on a big number, count the small marks past it. If the edge sits on the third small tick after the 6 cm mark, that's 6 cm and 3 mm, which is written as 6.3 cm.

sections.heading: Choosing the right tool
sections.body:
A **ruler** is great for small, straight things like a page or a pencil case. A **tape measure** is better for anything longer than your ruler, or for measuring around curves and corners, because it's flexible and can reach right across a room.

Most tape measures have a metal hook on the end that slides slightly — that's normal, it's built that way so the measurement is accurate whether you're hooking it over an edge or butting it up against a wall.

key_points: 10 mm = 1 cm, 100 cm = 1 m, and 1000 mm = 1 m.
Use millimetres for small or fiddly things, centimetres for medium objects, and metres for rooms or long items.
The small tick marks between the numbers on a ruler or tape measure are millimetres.
A tape measure's sliding hook is designed that way — it's not broken.
Measuring carefully the first time saves having to redo a job.
lessons.try_this: Grab a tape measure or ruler and measure five things around your home in centimetres — your foot, a door, a table, a book, and one thing you choose. Write down each measurement, then guess a sixth item's length before measuring it to check how close your guess was.

questions.prompt: There are 100 centimetres in 1 metre.
questions.explain: 1 metre is made up of 100 centimetres, which is why metre rulers and tape measures show numbers up to 100 in centimetres.

questions.prompt: Which tool is best for measuring the length of a hallway?
choices: Ruler
Tape measure
Kitchen scales
Measuring cup
questions.answer: Tape measure
questions.explain: A ruler is too short for a hallway. A tape measure is long, flexible, and designed for measuring longer distances.

questions.prompt: A screw gap measures 7 cm across. A hardware app wants the measurement entered in millimetres instead. What number should you enter?
questions.explain: There are 10 mm in every centimetre, so 7 cm x 10 = 70 mm.

questions.prompt: You measure a shelf gap and the tape shows 2.3 m. The cutting list needs it written in centimetres. What number goes on the list?
You look closely at a ruler and see lots of tiny lines between each centimetre number. What unit do those tiny lines measure?
questions.explain: Each small tick between the big centimetre numbers represents 1 millimetre, since 10 mm make up 1 cm.

questions.prompt: The materials list for a birdhouse says a gap needs to be exactly 3 millimetres. How would that unit normally be written using its short symbol?
questions.explain: Millimetre is shortened to mm, the same way centimetre is shortened to cm.

questions.prompt: A workshop plan lists a plank as 1.24 m long, but the cutting saw's dial only shows millimetres. What number should be set on the dial?
A pencil's tip lines up exactly halfway between the 6 cm and 7 cm marks on a ruler. How long is the pencil, in centimetres?
questions.explain: Halfway between 6 cm and 7 cm is 0.5 cm further than 6 cm, which is 6.5 cm.

questions.prompt: A tape measure's metal hook has come loose, so it slides an extra 3 mm past its resting point before the numbers start counting — every reading comes out 3 mm longer than the real length. The tape shows a doorframe as 204.6 cm wide. What is the doorframe's real width, in cm?
questions.explain: The faulty hook adds 3 mm (0.3 cm) to every reading, so the true width is the tape's reading minus that extra amount: 204.6 cm - 0.3 cm = 204.3 cm.

questions.prompt: Skirting board only comes in 2.4 m lengths, and every join has to land on a wall stud rather than butting two odd offcuts together — so each length used along a wall must be a fresh, uncut piece. You need to cover a straight wall run of 5.5 m. How many 2.4 m lengths do you need to buy?
questions.explain: Two lengths only give 2 x 2.4 m = 4.8 m, which is short of 5.5 m. A third length is needed to cover the rest, even though most of it goes to waste, so you must round up to 3.

questions.prompt: A tape measure's hook is deliberately made to slide back and forth by its own thickness. Imagine that hook was glued rigid instead, and you measured an inside width by pushing the rigid hook flat against a wall (rather than hooking it over an outside edge). Compared to the true length, would your reading come out too long or too short?
questions.explain: A sliding hook cancels out its own thickness whichever way it's used. A rigid hook pressed flat against a surface for an inside measurement would add its own thickness on top, making the reading too long.

questions.prompt: A shelf bracket's top screw hole needs to sit exactly 32.5 cm down from the top of a cupboard side panel that is 72 cm tall overall. If you measure up from the bottom of the panel instead of down from the top, at what distance from the bottom should that same hole line up, in cm?
questions.explain: The hole sits 32.5 cm down from the top, so it is 72 cm - 32.5 cm = 39.5 cm up from the bottom. Measuring from the wrong edge without redoing this sum puts the hole in the wrong spot entirely.

activity.title: Measure a real tabletop for a trim job
activity.why: Proves they can take a genuine measurement two different ways, notice if the two disagree, and use the result in a real calculation rather than just reading a single number off a tape.
steps: Choose a rectangular object at home — a tabletop, door, or the top of a box — and measure its length and width with a tape measure, to the nearest millimetre.
Measure the same two sides again using only the ruler, moving it along in short sections and adding the sections together if the ruler is shorter than the object.
Compare your two sets of measurements and note whether the tape measure and the ruler agreed.
Calculate the perimeter by adding all four sides together (length + width + length + width).
Imagine running a strip of trim all the way around the edge of the object, and work out how many centimetres of trim that would take in total.
Record your results below.

record.label: Length of the object, in cm (tape measure)
Width of the object, in cm (tape measure)
Total perimeter (all four sides added up), in cm
Did the tape measure and ruler agree? What did you do if they didn't?

activity.check: The perimeter should equal 2 x (length + width) from the two measured sides. The tape and ruler readings should be within a few millimetres of each other — if they're wildly different, something was measured wrong.

lessons.title: The hand tool kit: what each common tool is for and how to hold it safely
lessons.intro: Open up almost any toolbox in Cooktown and you'll find the same handful of tools doing most of the work. Let's meet them, and learn how to hold each one properly.

sections.heading: The everyday tool box
sections.body:
Most home jobs only need a small set of hand tools: a **screwdriver**, a **hammer**, **pliers**, and an **adjustable spanner** (often called a **shifter**). Each one is built for a particular job, and using the right tool makes the job easier and safer.

This lesson is about hand tools you can use with an adult keeping an eye on you. Power tools are a different story — they're always an adult's job to operate, even though you might help hold or hand things over.

sections.heading: Screwdrivers: Phillips head and flathead
sections.body:
A **Phillips head** screwdriver has a cross-shaped tip that fits into a cross-shaped slot in the screw. A **flathead** screwdriver has a flat blade tip that fits a straight slot.

Using the wrong driver on a screw makes it slip and can chew up the screw head or scratch whatever you're working on. Before you start, look closely at the screw's slot and pick the driver that matches it exactly.

sections.heading: Hammers, pliers and the shifter
sections.body:
A **hammer** drives nails in with a swinging strike. **Pliers** grip, hold or bend things — handy for gripping a nail to pull it out, or bending a piece of wire. A **shifter** (adjustable spanner) opens and closes to fit different sized nuts and bolts, so you can turn them tight or loosen them.

Each tool does one job well. Trying to use pliers as a hammer, or a screwdriver as a lever, usually ends with a slipped tool and a sore hand.

sections.heading: Holding tools safely
sections.body:
For a controlled hammer swing, hold the handle nearer the end, not right up against the head — this gives you better control and more power with less effort. Keep your other hand well clear of where the hammer will land.

When using a screwdriver, keep the point aimed away from your body and hold the item steady. With pliers, keep your fingers clear of the pivot point in the middle where they could get pinched.

- Point sharp or pointed tools away from people
- Put a tool down flat when you're not using it, rather than leaving it balanced on an edge
- Ask an adult before using any tool you haven't used before

key_points: Phillips head screwdrivers have a cross-shaped tip; flathead screwdrivers have a flat blade.
A shifter (adjustable spanner) is used to turn nuts and bolts.
Pliers grip and bend; a hammer drives nails.
Hold a hammer's handle near the end for better control, and keep your other hand clear of the strike zone.
Power tools are always an adult's job to operate.
lessons.try_this: With an adult, go through a household toolbox or junk drawer and sort what you find into groups: screwdrivers, gripping tools, hammering tools, and spanners. For any screws you can see around the house (on switch plates, hinges, furniture), work out whether they're Phillips head or flathead without undoing them.

questions.prompt: A Phillips head screwdriver has a cross-shaped tip.
questions.explain: A Phillips head screwdriver's tip is shaped like a cross, matching screws with a cross-shaped slot.

questions.prompt: Which tool would you use to tighten a nut onto a bolt?
choices: Hammer
Shifter (adjustable spanner)
Tape measure
Paintbrush
questions.answer: Shifter (adjustable spanner)
questions.explain: A shifter's jaws adjust to fit around a nut so it can be turned tight or loosened.

questions.prompt: You try to undo a screw with a screwdriver that doesn't match its slot, and it slips sideways instead of turning. Why does matching the driver to the screw matter?
choices: So the driver grips the screw properly and doesn't slip or damage it
Because flathead screwdrivers are always faster
Because Phillips head screws are illegal to use with flatheads
It doesn't actually matter
questions.answer: So the driver grips the screw properly and doesn't slip or damage it
questions.explain: A matching driver sits firmly in the screw's slot. A mismatched driver can slip, damaging the screw head or whatever you're working on.

questions.prompt: Grandpa always grips his hammer near the very end of the handle, not close to the head. Does that give him better control of the swing?
questions.explain: Holding near the end of the handle gives a more controlled, powerful swing and keeps your hand further from where the hammer strikes.

questions.prompt: You need to tighten a nut, and reach for the tool with jaws that adjust to fit different sized nuts and bolts. What's the everyday tradie nickname for this tool?
questions.explain: An adjustable spanner is commonly called a shifter because its jaws shift to fit different sized nuts and bolts.

questions.prompt: You need to bend a length of wire into a hook shape and hold it steady while you do. Which everyday tool is actually built for gripping and bending like this?
questions.explain: Pliers are designed to grip firmly and can bend wire or small objects that are hard to hold with fingers alone.

questions.prompt: You're about to swing a hammer at a nail, and your little brother is standing right where the hammer will swing. What should you do before you start?
questions.explain: Checking the space around you before you swing a tool is always the safest first step, even if you plan to be careful.

questions.prompt: Jake wants to pry open a paint tin lid with his flathead screwdriver instead of grabbing a proper tool for the job. Is that a safe way to use the screwdriver?
questions.explain: Screwdrivers aren't built to be levered or hit like a chisel. Doing this can snap the tip or make it slip, which can cause an injury. Use the tool actually made for the job.

questions.prompt: You're assembling a cubby house that needs 20 coach screws, all driven with a Phillips head screwdriver. Coach screws are only sold in packets of 8. How many packets do you need to buy?
questions.explain: Two packets only give 16 screws, which is short of the 20 needed. A third packet is needed to cover the rest, so you round up to 3, even though 4 screws will be left over.

questions.prompt: You've matched a Phillips head driver to a Phillips head screw, but the tip keeps slipping out of the slot no matter how hard you push. The type of driver is right. What should you check next about the driver?
questions.explain: Phillips head drivers come in different sizes (like PH1 and PH2), and a driver that's the right type but the wrong size will still slip and chew up the screw. Checking the size is the next thing to try.

questions.prompt: A shifter's jaw opens to a maximum of 24 mm. You need to loosen a nut that measures 19 mm across the flats, but years of paint have built up around it, adding roughly 2 mm of extra thickness all around. How many millimetres of clearance will be left once the shifter is opened to fit over the painted nut?
questions.explain: The paint adds 2 mm to the nut's effective size: 19 mm + 2 mm = 21 mm. The shifter opens to 24 mm, so the clearance left is 24 mm - 21 mm = 3 mm.

questions.prompt: You're using a hammer's claw to pull out a bent nail, but the timber underneath is starting to crack as you pull. What should you place under the hammer's head to protect the wood and give you better leverage?
questions.explain: Placing a scrap block of wood under the hammer's head spreads the pressure over a wider area (protecting the timber) and gives the claw a higher pivot point, which increases your leverage on the nail.

activity.title: Tool audit and shifter fit-test
activity.why: Proves they can sort real tools by function, and actually measure and compare a tool's capability (a shifter's jaw opening) against real hardware instead of just naming tools.
steps: With an adult, gather the household toolbox or tool drawer.
Sort every tool you find into four piles: screwdrivers, gripping tools, hammering tools, spanners/shifters.
Count the total number of tools across all four piles.
Find three different nuts, bolts, or hex heads around the house (a garden tap, a bike, a piece of furniture) and use the ruler to measure the widest one across its flats, in millimetres.
Open the shifter's jaw against your ruler and check whether it's wide enough to fit around each of the three items you found.
Pick one screw you can see without undoing it, and work out whether it needs a Phillips head or flathead driver just by looking closely at its slot.
Record your results below.

record.label: Total number of tools you sorted
Width across the flats of the widest nut/bolt/hex head you measured, in mm
How many of the three items did the shifter's jaw fit around?
What did you learn about matching a driver's size to a screw, from the one you looked at?

activity.check: A typical household toolbox has somewhere between 5 and 30 tools. The widest nut/bolt measured should be a plausible everyday size — most household hardware sits well under 25 mm across the flats.

lessons.title: Screws, nails, nuts and bolts: which fastener for which job
lessons.intro: Screws, nails, nuts and bolts all do the same basic job — holding two things together — but they're not interchangeable. Picking the right one makes a build stronger and easier to fix later.

sections.heading: Why fasteners matter
sections.body: A **fastener** is anything used to join two materials together. Different fasteners hold in different ways, come apart (or don't) in different ways, and suit different materials. Choosing the right one is part of planning a build properly.

sections.heading: Nails vs screws
sections.body:
A **nail** is a smooth metal spike driven in with a hammer. It's quick to put in, but it can pull out more easily and isn't meant to be removed and reused.

A **screw** has a spiral thread and is driven in with a screwdriver (or a drill, when an adult is using one). Screws generally hold more strongly than nails of a similar size, and they can be undone again if you need to take something apart.

sections.heading: Nuts and bolts
sections.body:
A **bolt** is a threaded rod, usually with a head on one end. A **nut** is a small block with a matching thread that screws onto the bolt to clamp two things together. A **washer** — a flat metal ring — often sits under the nut or bolt head to spread the load evenly.

Nuts and bolts are great for jobs that might need to come apart later, like flat-pack furniture, bike parts, or a trailer that gets serviced.

example.prompt: You're building flat-pack furniture that the family might need to move house with one day and take apart again. Which fastener type makes the most sense?
working: Nuts and bolts can be tightened firmly and undone again
This makes them ideal for furniture that may need disassembling later

sections.heading: Picking the right fastener
sections.body:
Ask yourself: does this need to come apart again? Is it wood, metal, or something else? Does it need to hold a heavy load, or just something light?

For quick wood-to-wood joins that won't be taken apart, nails often do the job. For anything that needs real strength or might be undone later, screws or nuts and bolts are the better choice.

key_points: A nut screws onto the threads of a bolt to clamp materials together.
Screws generally hold more strongly than nails and can be undone again.
Nails are quick for simple wood joins that won't need to come apart.
A washer spreads the load under a nut or bolt head.
Choosing a fastener depends on the material, the strength needed, and whether it needs to come apart later.
lessons.try_this: With an adult's permission, look around the house for five different fasteners — on furniture, door hinges, a bike, or in a junk drawer. For each one, decide whether it's a nail, screw, nut, bolt, or washer, and guess why that fastener was chosen for that job.

questions.prompt: A nut screws onto the threads of a bolt.
questions.explain: A nut has a matching internal thread that screws onto a bolt's external thread, clamping materials together.

questions.prompt: Which fastener is best for joining two pieces of flat-pack furniture that might need to come apart later?
choices: Nail
Nut and bolt
Staple
Glue
questions.answer: Nut and bolt
questions.explain: A nut and bolt can be tightened firmly and then undone again later, which suits furniture that may be moved or reassembled.

questions.prompt: You notice a thin metal ring sitting under a bolt head, between it and the wood. What job is it doing there?
choices: To spread the load under a nut or bolt head so it doesn't dig into the material
To make the bolt longer
To colour-match the screw
To replace a nut
questions.answer: To spread the load under a nut or bolt head so it doesn't dig into the material
questions.explain: A washer is a flat ring that spreads out the pressure from a nut or bolt head, protecting the surface underneath.

questions.prompt: Dad chooses screws instead of nails for a garden box that'll get knocked around a lot. Do screws generally hold two pieces of wood together more strongly than similar-sized nails?
questions.explain: A screw's spiral thread grips the wood fibres along its whole length, which usually holds more strongly than a smooth nail.

questions.prompt: Under the bolt head on a bike rack, there's a thin flat metal ring spreading out the pressure so it doesn't dig into the metal. What's this ring called?
questions.explain: A washer sits under the nut or bolt head and spreads the clamping force over a wider area.

questions.prompt: A hardware packet is laid out as 4 rows of screws, 6 to a row. How many screws does the packet actually contain?
questions.explain: 4 rows of 6 screws is 4 x 6 = 24 screws.

questions.prompt: You're helping build a garden trellis that'll stay in one spot forever and never need to come apart. For a quick wood-to-wood join like this, which everyday fastener makes the most sense?
questions.explain: For a simple wood join that won't need to be undone, nails are quick and do the job well.

questions.prompt: You're building a bike rack from steel tubing that might need adjusting or repairing down the track. Why would a nut and bolt make more sense here than a nail?
choices: It can be tightened firmly and undone again for adjustments or repairs
It's always cheaper than a nail
It doesn't need a spanner
Bolts can't be used with metal
questions.answer: It can be tightened firmly and undone again for adjustments or repairs
questions.explain: Nuts and bolts suit metal builds that might need adjusting or repairing later, since they can be loosened and retightened.

questions.prompt: You're building deck rail sections. Each section uses 6 bolts, and each bolt needs 2 washers. A bag has 100 washers in it. How many complete sections can you build before the washers run out?
questions.explain: Each section needs 6 x 2 = 12 washers. 100 washers divided by 12 per section is 8.33, so only 8 whole sections can be built (with 4 washers left over) before running out.

questions.prompt: A nail was hammered into a piece of decking to join two boards, but after a few weeks of wind and movement the boards keep working loose and the nail heads are popping up above the surface. Which fastener should replace the nails to actually fix this, since the boards keep flexing?
questions.explain: A screw's spiral thread bites into the wood fibres along its whole length, which resists the repeated flexing that gradually backs a smooth nail straight out.

questions.prompt: A gate hinge keeps working loose because the wood around the screw hole has worn soft and spongy, so the screw just spins in the hole without gripping. Putting in a longer screw of the same width doesn't help. What kind of fastener change would actually fix this?
questions.explain: Passing a bolt right through both sides and clamping it with a washer and nut on the far side doesn't rely on grip in the worn-out wood at all, unlike a screw that only holds if the timber around it is solid.

questions.prompt: A steel bolt holding a swing seat's chain has been outside for two years. It now looks pitted and reddish-brown, and the nut barely turns when you try to check it. What does this mean, and what should happen before it's trusted with weight again?
choices: Rust has weakened it — replace it with new galvanised or stainless hardware
It's just dirty — a wipe with a cloth will fix it
Steel bolts never rust, so it's fine as is
Paint over it and reuse it straight away
questions.answer: Rust has weakened it — replace it with new galvanised or stainless hardware
questions.explain: Pitting and a seized nut are signs the metal has corroded and lost strength. A fastener holding weight, especially a child's, should be replaced with new rust-resistant hardware rather than patched up.

activity.title: Fastener sort and washer test
activity.why: Proves they can identify real fasteners by handling them, and actually test (not just recite) what a washer does by comparing a real result with and without one.
materials: assorted nuts, bolts, washers, screws and nails from a junk drawer or shed
a piece of cardboard or thick foam
steps: With an adult, collect at least 10 mixed fasteners from a junk drawer, shed or toolbox — nails, screws, nuts, bolts and washers.
Sort them into groups and count how many of each type you found.
Take one bolt and nut. Sandwich two layers of cardboard between the bolt head and the nut with no washer, and tighten by hand or with the shifter until snug.
Undo it, then repeat with a washer under the nut, tightening it by the same amount.
Measure the diameter of the dent left in the cardboard each time with the ruler, in millimetres.
Compare the two dents and write down what you noticed.
Record your results below.

record.label: Total number of fasteners you sorted
Diameter of the dent in the cardboard without a washer, in mm
Diameter of the dent in the cardboard with a washer, in mm
What was different about the two dents, and why do you think that happened?

activity.check: The dent made with a washer should be spread over a wider, shallower area matching the washer's shape, while the dent without one is usually smaller and more sharply cut by the nut's edges alone.

lessons.title: Following instructions and a materials list: flat-pack, model kit or recipe
lessons.intro: Flat-pack furniture, model kits and recipes all come with instructions for a reason. Reading them properly, in order, is a skill on its own — and it saves a lot of frustration.

sections.heading: Why instructions have an order
sections.body: Instructions are written in the order they need to happen. Step 3 often depends on step 2 being done correctly. Skipping ahead, or doing steps out of order, can mean a part gets stuck, glued the wrong way, or left out completely.

sections.heading: Reading the materials list before you start
sections.body:
Most kits, flat-packs and recipes start with a **materials list** (sometimes called a parts list or ingredients list). This tells you everything you'll need and how much of it.

Before you begin, lay everything out and check it against the list. It's much easier to notice a missing part now than halfway through the build.

sections.heading: Step by step, not skipping ahead
sections.body: Read a whole step before you start doing it, not just the first few words. Gather any tools that step needs before you begin. Going slowly and checking each step as you finish it is faster in the end than rushing and having to undo a mistake.

example.prompt: A birdhouse kit's materials list needs 4 identical panels, using 3 screws per panel. You've already fitted 2 panels. How many screws have you used so far?

sections.heading: What to do when something doesn't fit
sections.body: If a part doesn't fit or a step doesn't make sense, stop. Don't force it — forcing a part can break it or bend something out of shape. Go back and check the step before, make sure you have the right piece, and ask an adult if you're still stuck.

key_points: Instructions are written in order because later steps often depend on earlier ones.
Check the materials list against your parts before you start.
Read a whole step before doing it, and gather the tools it needs first.
If something doesn't fit, stop and check rather than forcing it.
Going slowly and checking your work is usually faster than rushing and fixing mistakes.
lessons.try_this: Pick a simple recipe, model kit, or piece of flat-pack furniture at home. Read through the whole materials list first and tick off each item as you find it, before doing a single step. If you don't have an actual kit handy, do this with a recipe from a cookbook instead.

questions.prompt: It's a good idea to check all the parts against the materials list before you start building.
questions.explain: Checking the materials list first means you'll notice a missing part before it becomes a problem partway through.

questions.prompt: Before starting a flat-pack furniture build, what should you do first?
choices: Lay out all the parts and check them against the materials list
Start screwing pieces together randomly
Throw away the instructions
Skip to the last step
questions.answer: Lay out all the parts and check them against the materials list
questions.explain: Laying out and checking parts first means you'll spot anything missing or extra before you start, saving time later.

questions.prompt: You count the screws in a birdhouse kit's bag and find only 6, but the materials list says you need 8. What's the smart move?
choices: Stop and check with an adult before continuing, in case parts are missing
Use nails instead without telling anyone
Just build it with 6 and hope it holds
Throw the whole kit away
questions.answer: Stop and check with an adult before continuing, in case parts are missing
questions.explain: Missing parts are worth flagging early. An adult might find spares, check the bag again, or contact the supplier.

questions.prompt: A birdhouse kit needs 3 screws for each of its 4 identical panels. You've fitted 2 panels so far. How many screws have you used up to this point?
questions.explain: Each panel uses 3 screws, so 2 panels use 2 x 3 = 6 screws.

questions.prompt: A panel won't quite slot into place on a model kit. Jake decides to push harder rather than stop and check. Is forcing it the right call?
questions.explain: Forcing a part that doesn't fit can break it or bend it out of shape. It's better to stop and check what went wrong.

questions.prompt: Before starting a flat-pack build, you check the page at the front that lists every part and how many of each you'll need. What's that page called?
questions.explain: This is usually called a materials list or parts list, and it's worth checking before you start building.

questions.prompt: Halfway through following a recipe, you realise a later step needs flour measured out - something you haven't done yet. What should you have done differently from the start?
choices: Read the whole recipe first so you understand the order before you start
Just start and figure it out as you go
Skip the flour step entirely
Double the sugar to compensate
questions.answer: Read the whole recipe first so you understand the order before you start
questions.explain: Reading the whole recipe first means you won't be caught out partway through, scrambling to measure something at the last second.

questions.prompt: Following a 10-step model kit, step 6 asks you to glue a part that step 4 was meant to have already attached. What's the smartest thing to check before gluing anything?
choices: Go back and make sure step 4 was actually completed correctly before continuing
Ignore it and keep going forward
Start again from step 1 without checking anything
Use extra glue to fix it later
questions.answer: Go back and make sure step 4 was actually completed correctly before continuing
questions.explain: When a later step assumes something earlier was done, it's worth going back to check rather than pushing on and hoping.

questions.prompt: A model kit's instructions say each of 6 identical wings needs 4 rivets. The rivet bag only has 20 rivets in it. How many complete wings can you build before the rivets run out?
questions.explain: Each wing needs 4 rivets. 20 rivets divided by 4 per wing is exactly 5, so you can complete 5 whole wings before running out, one short of the full 6.

questions.prompt: A fence kit's instructions describe 7 identical panels. Attaching the first panel (following steps 2-4 carefully for the first time) takes 6 minutes. Each panel after that only takes 4 minutes, because you already know the process. How many minutes in total will all 7 panels take?
questions.explain: The first panel takes 6 minutes. The remaining 6 panels take 4 minutes each: 6 x 4 = 24 minutes. Total time = 6 + 24 = 30 minutes.

questions.prompt: A flat-pack wardrobe's materials list needs 32 identical cam bolts, packed 8 to a bag. You count the bags already in the box: there are 3 full bags plus 5 loose bolts. How many bolts are missing from the full order?
questions.explain: 3 full bags give 3 x 8 = 24 bolts, plus 5 loose bolts is 29 bolts in total. The order needs 32, so 32 - 29 = 3 bolts are missing.

questions.prompt: A recipe says 'bake for 25 minutes at 180°C', but after 15 minutes you notice the oven dial has actually been set to 160°C the whole time because you misread it earlier. Once you fix the temperature, what should happen to the total baking time compared to the original plan?
questions.explain: Baking at a lower temperature than planned means the food has cooked more slowly than intended, so the total time in the oven needs to be extended once the temperature is corrected, not left at the original 25 minutes.

activity.title: Full materials-check and timed build
activity.why: Proves they can run a real build end-to-end the proper way — checking the materials list first, timing the actual work, and comparing that to their own prediction.
materials: a simple model kit, flat-pack item, or a no-cook recipe (like a wrap, sandwich or trail mix)
a clock, watch or phone timer
steps: Choose a simple model kit, flat-pack item, or a no-cook recipe (like a wrap, sandwich or trail mix) that you can finish today, working from a full materials or ingredients list.
Before starting, write down or list every material, part or ingredient it needs.
Guess how many minutes you think the whole thing will take, and write your guess down.
Check every item off the list, noting anything missing or needing a substitute.
Start a timer, then follow the steps in order without skipping ahead.
Stop the timer the moment you finish, and record the total number of minutes it actually took.
Record your results below, including anything that didn't fit or need fixing along the way.
